extracted.intended_audience: television comedy writers, sitcom writers, and aspiring comedy/humor writers
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and informal standards for writing jokes and scenes for television sitcoms (and transferable short-form comedic writing), focused on avoiding predictability and improving originality, timing, and character-driven humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule of 2's
rubrics_metrics.description: If the writing staff was working on a joke and any two writers pitched essentially the same punchline we automatically discarded it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this as a hard discipline: discard a punchline if two writers independently arrive at the same line — no debate, even if it seems funny. Rationale: if two writers can come up with it, some audience members can too; therefore it's predictable and should be jettisoned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid predictable/obvious punchlines
rubrics_metrics.description: If I can predict a joke it's just lazy writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the audience or a seasoned writer can anticipate the punchline, the joke is weak. Seek angles that aren't immediate or obvious; do not settle for the first automatic laugh line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dig deeper beyond the first punchline
rubrics_metrics.description: When you’re trying to come up with a joke sometimes your first punchline might be the obvious one. Learn to dig deeper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After the first (obvious) punchline, keep brainstorming: ask whether there's a better, fresher, more unexpected, or 'out in left field' joke. Spending more time often yields stronger, less derivative choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for surprise / unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: There will still be jokes that surprise you and make you laugh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comedy catches the audience unprepared in a way that still makes narrative sense. Prefer surprises over predictable callbacks or ironies that the audience already sees coming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid catch-phrases and recycled lines
rubrics_metrics.description: They often resort to irony so it’s not even jokes. It’s catch-phrases or 'Gee, THAT went well.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of using hackneyed catch-phrases or lines that sound like stock reactions. These feel safe but are readily anticipated by savvy audiences and weaken humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect audience sophistication (sitcom-savvy viewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Because sitcom audiences are more sitcom savvy your job is much harder now than it was back when we were writing CHEERS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write with the modern, media-literate viewer in mind. Jokes must be smarter or less obvious to surprise an audience accustomed to many sitcom conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write to be the best in your genre / know your show's aim
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every show is CHEERS or is even going for the type of humor we went for. But you can strive to be the best in your genre, whatever it is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor standards to the show's tone and audience expectations, but within that frame, pursue higher-quality, less lazy humor. Examples: a Disney Channel sitcom can still be superior to its peers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-driven humor: create compelling, flawed characters
rubrics_metrics.description: The characters need to be compelling on some level, more than just generic types who serve as joke-conduits. Something flawed but expansive needs to be in their character makeup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build characters with depth and specific flaws so jokes arise naturally from character, not just from archetypal gags. Make audiences care enough about backstory to enhance jokes, but preserve some mystique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and connection: timing is everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Timing is everything. But they have to connect in way that is familiar on one hand, but throw a curveball every now and then too, yet still stay on point and in character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver jokes with precise timing so the set-up feels familiar enough to register, then deliver an unexpected payoff. Maintain relevance to scene and character so the surprise doesn't feel out-of-place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject client/performer insertions of clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: I've seen clients insert the most mangy cliches you can imagine into stuff I'm trying to fix... They couldn't recognize humor unless they'd already heard the line before.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guard against people (clients, performers) who replace better material with comfortable, familiar lines. Educate or push back to preserve originality and avoid defaulting to what 'feels funny' to an untrained ear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply the principles across formats (blogs, social, short-form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Good feedback that can be applied in so many ways beyond comedy writing for a TV show... I use this sort of idea when updating my humor blog and when making silly posts on Instagram, Twitter, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The core standards — avoid obviousness, seek surprise, respect audience sophistication, and spend time finding fresh angles — apply to short-form and social-media humor as well. Walk the fine line between 'safe' humor and originality.
